title: How We Built Zeta2: Training an Edit Prediction Model in Production — Ben Kunkle, Zed

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is training a specialized student model via teacher-student distillation, including repair, settled-data validation, and filtering for ideal training examples. The system is an IDE edit-prediction assistant within Zed, a developer-platform coding tool. The talk covers production data capture, distillation and repair for data preparation, student model training, offline evaluation with custom metrics, and traffic-sampled deployment. Requires familiarity with model training and distillation concepts but remains accessible to applied practitioners. A structured conference presentation with distinct sections covering pipeline, evaluation, and deployment. summary: Ben Kunkle, edit predictions lead at Zed, describes the training pipeline for Zed 2, a small specialized model fine-tuned to predict the next code edit given surrounding context including recent edits, cursor position, type definitions, and diagnostics. Because it runs on every keystroke, speed is critical, making a small fine-tuned model ideal. The pipeline begins with opt-in production data captured as snapshots, preserving all contextual information. A frontier teacher model generates predictions via distillation, but this is noisy — asking 100,000 times yields many different answers, requiring careful prompt tuning. Predictions failing heuristic checks (e.g., undoing what was typed, ignoring editable region boundaries) go through a repair step using a second frontier model call. Up through repair, outputs are cached and reusable across experiments; experiment-specific prompt formatting then adapts teacher outputs to the student's desired format. The entire pipeline uses JSONL files where each stage adds or rearranges fields. A key innovation is settled data: since Zed is the editor, they can wait until a user stops editing a region (roughly 10 seconds of inactivity), snapshot it, and use it as ground truth. This is noisy — users may change their mind or agents may rewrite code — so they filter by generating multiple predictions and checking if any are close to the settled state via Levenshtein distance. Originally this required 10 teacher predictions per example (a million frontier requests for 100K examples), which was prohibitively expensive. Since Zed 2 now approaches teacher quality, they run the student checkpoint 50 times instead at negligible cost. Ideal training examples fall in the middle of the distance distribution: too close is obvious, too far is noise, but the middle captures novel content past the student's training cutoff. Offline evaluations use a held-out test set, tracking delta CARF (an n-gram comparison metric), reversal ratio (undoing exactly what was typed), kept rate in production, and diagnostic error counts. Production experiments are deployed with traffic sampling (e.g., 15%) before full rollout.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Edit Prediction Concept
sections.summary: Ben Kunkle introduces himself as edit predictions lead at Zed and explains edit prediction: giving a model the code region around the cursor plus context (recent edits, cursor position, type definitions, diagnostics) to predict the next edit. It runs on every keystroke, making a small specialized fine-tuned model ideal.

sections.title: Pipeline - Distillation and Repair Step
sections.summary: The pipeline starts with opt-in production snapshots capturing all contextual data. A frontier teacher model generates predictions via distillation, but outputs are noisy and require prompt tuning. Predictions failing heuristic checks (undoing typed text, ignoring region boundaries) are sent to a second frontier model for repair. Outputs through the repair stage are cached and reusable across experiments.

sections.title: Prompt Formatting and Pipeline Architecture
sections.summary: Experiment-specific prompt formatting adapts cached teacher outputs to the student's desired format (e.g., whether to include diagnostics, how much edit history). The pipeline uses JSONL files where each stage adds or rearranges fields. Training typically uses 100,000 examples at peak, 10-50K for smaller experiments.

sections.title: Settled Data and Validation Filtering
sections.summary: Settled data captures the final state after a user stops editing a region (10-second inactivity heuristic), providing ground truth. This is noisy due to mind changes or agent rewrites. Filtering generates multiple predictions and checks Levenshtein distance to the settled state. Originally requiring 10 teacher predictions per example (1 million frontier requests for 100K examples), this was prohibitively expensive. Since Zed 2 approaches teacher quality, they now run the student checkpoint 50 times at negligible cost.

sections.title: Ideal Training Examples and Levenshtein Distribution
sections.summary: Ideal training examples fall in the middle of the Levenshtein distance distribution: too close to settled state is obvious, too far is noise, but the middle captures nearly-correct predictions including novel content past the student's training cutoff. They train on the closest prediction rather than the settled state itself due to residual noise.

sections.title: Offline Evaluations and Metrics
sections.summary: Offline evals use a held-out test set and compare against 3 teacher predictions (since many edits have multiple valid answers). Metrics include delta CARF (n-gram comparison), reversal ratio (undoing exactly what was typed), kept rate in production, and diagnostic error counts (errors before vs. after prediction).

sections.title: Production Deployment and Q&A
sections.summary: Experiments are deployed with traffic sampling (e.g., 15%) before full rollout, monitored via a dashboard tracking acceptance rate and latency. The released model is V0211 seed coder. In Q&A, Ben confirms the settled state heuristic is simply 10 seconds of editing inactivity, not git commits.
